Lessons.Title: Multiply More Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U05:L21 asks pupils to multiply two tenths-based decimal factors or whole×hundredths and explain equivalence using whole-number product TIMES the product of decimal units. The student chooses strategies, not an arbitrary formula for moving decimal points.

Warm-up Estimation Exploration Central Park gives about3.85km length and0.79km width and asks too-low/about-right/too-high estimates for area. The literal rectangle multiplication3.85×0.79=3.0415km² is only a rectangular MODEL of irregular park shape; source credited MapMaster CC-BY-SA map art not independently copied. Teacher evaluates sensible estimates and geographic limitations.

Activity1 original equivalent expressions7.2×5.3=(72×53)×0.01=38.16;6.5×2.8=(65×28)÷100=18.20;31×0.44=(31×44)×1/100=13.64. Explain why each unit product is a hundredth and compute whole product without decimal-place guesswork.
Activity2 Choose Your Strategy original7.3×4.2=30.66,38×0.55=20.9,285×0.17=48.45. Strategies include whole-number facts, distributivity and compensation; teacher assesses rationale and units.

Previous fictional6.4×2.7 and235×.18 are valid Edulytiks extensions only. Numeric selected source Practice cannot grade original Central Park estimate, map or explanation. Independently authored Cool-down separate from gated publisher original.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: extend place-value multiplication to two tenths-based decimal factors and large whole-number-by-hundredths products, explaining WHY equivalent integer-product expressions represent the same value. The 2021 source requires justification of equivalence before exact computation, then independent strategy selection.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up — benchmark: decide whether 6.4×2.7 is between12 and24 by comparing 6.4 with6 and7 and 2.7 with2 and3. An estimate near17 is reasonable, but an actual value needs a correct count of hundredths or decimal partial products.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — prove equivalence: calculate 6.4×2.7 as (64×27)×0.01, because both factors were written as tenths and 0.1×0.1=0.01. Multiply64×27=1728 to get17.28. Also calculate 5.6×3.2=(56×32)÷100=17.92 and 23×0.47=(23×47)×0.01=10.81. Explain what fractional unit each whole-number product counts rather than merely inserting decimal punctuation.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — choose your strategy: calculate 8.2×3.4=27.88 using partial products or 82×34 hundredths. Calculate 47×0.36=16.92. An extra 3-digit challenge is 235×0.18=42.30; show why the hundreds-place integer factor increases computation size but not the decimal unit used for the other factor.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: open justification of equivalent expressions, independent method choice and comparison of solutions require teacher review. Numeric results and decimal-place constraints can be checked, but a guessed decimal point without unit reasoning cannot prove the source learner task.

Lessons.Title: Divide Whole Numbers by 0.1 and 0.01 PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U05:L22 asks how many equal groups OF SIZE0.1 or0.01 fit within a WHOLE NUMBER; this is not sharing whole number across10 students. Use a consistent one-whole hundredths grid.
Warm-up original Number Talk1÷1/10=10,2÷1/10=20,1÷0.01=100,2÷0.01=200. Students compare unit fraction denominators to count the corresponding groups.

Activity1 Patterns in Dividing by Decimal Units: original source3÷0.1=30,3÷0.01=300,4÷0.1=40 and4÷0.01=400. One whole contains10 tenths or100 hundredths; multiplying by whole dividend counts groups. Original pupils may use grid pictures.

Activity2 Divide Whole Numbers by Decimals asks students to describe the GENERAL rule for any whole number divided by0.1 and0.01 and explain through units and inverse multiplication, not just output another fixed problem. Student explanations and original diagrams require teacher review.
Previous valid first-party invented7÷0.1/0.01 remain optional extensions. Source gated Cool-down cannot be claimed recovered; independently authored teacher Cool-down uses5 whole squares.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: discover and explain the pattern in the NUMBER of tenths or hundredths contained in positive whole quantities, not memorize an unexplained rule for sliding decimal points. The 2021 lesson first builds an individual-grid pattern from three and four wholes and then generalizes to any whole number with partner revision.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: look at a first-party original one-unit square divided into ten equal rows and each row into ten equal cells. Label each row as one tenth and each small cell as one hundredth. Count 10 rows or 100 individual small cells without changing the unit whole.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — count several wholes: three wholes have30 tenths or300 hundredths, so3÷0.1=30 and3÷0.01=300. Four whole-unit squares similarly contain40 tenths or400 hundredths. Draw a single grid and explain how the count scales by the number of identical wholes instead of drawing four separate pictures when the conceptual unit is already understood.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — formulate a general rule: for a positive whole number n, n÷0.1 equals10n and n÷0.01 equals100n. Use an independently chosen n such as seven and justify the values70 and700 by repeatedly counting pieces in one whole. Explain why dividing by a positive number less than one can yield a greater numerical quotient.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: the original teacher tasks include an initial visual pattern, a student-authored general explanation, partner critique and revision. A check of n×10 or n×100 alone is not full source-task parity; teacher reviews the grid and reasoning.

KeyConcepts.Title: Division by a small positive group size
KeyConcepts.Definition: Smaller group sizes require more groups from a fixed positive total.
KeyConcepts.Example: Seven wholes contain700 hundredths and70 tenths.

Lessons.Title: Divide Whole Numbers by Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U05:L23 extends whole dividend divided by unit decimal0.1/0.01 to ANY number of tenths or hundredths less than one. Explain grouping models, the inverse multiplication check and the pattern with fixed divisor.
Warm-up original True/False:6÷0.01=60 FALSE (600),6÷0.1<6÷0.01 TRUE (60<600),6÷0.01=60÷0.1 TRUE (both600). Learners explain differences between decimal units of ten-to-one size.

Activity1 Same Divisor Different Dividend source1÷0.2=5,2÷0.2=10,3÷0.2=15,4÷0.2=20; source1÷0.02=50,2÷0.02=100,3÷0.02=150,4÷0.02=200. Observe how each whole adds five 0.2-sized groups or50 0.02-sized groups.

Activity2 Evaluate Expressions source12÷0.2=60 with Tyler's source shaded-hundredths grid and algebraic relation12×(1÷0.2)=12×5=60. Also original14÷0.5=28 and5÷0.25=20. Source student explanation and pictured blue/orange grouping require teacher review.

Previous independent extra division examples retained only as optional; the bounded exact digital Practice does not pretend to verify Tyler's source drawing or open peer explanation. Independent Edulytiks cooldown uses9÷0.3.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: count how many groups of a decimal less than one fit into a whole number, extending the prior lesson from unit tenths and hundredths to 0.2, 0.02, 0.5 and 0.25. The source first varies the whole dividend with a fixed decimal divisor and asks learners to explain pattern relationships, then uses an economical one-whole model to solve a larger dividend.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare 1÷0.2 and1÷0.02 using one hundredths grid. Five groups of0.2 fit into one whole, while fifty groups of0.02 fit into one whole. Distinguish counting exact repeated portions from ordinary division of a fraction among more people.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — fixed divisor: for 0.2-sized groups, 1,2,3,4 whole units contain 5,10,15,20 groups. For0.02-sized groups, they contain50,100,150,200 groups. Describe the ten-to-one relationship between counts for these two group sizes, using first-party diagrams or a verbally labeled row of hundredths.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — use a one-whole fact: calculate 12÷0.2 by knowing five 0.2-sized groups fit into one whole, then multiply twelve by five to get60. For 14÷0.5=28, note two half-sized groups per whole. For5÷0.25=20, note four quarter-sized groups per whole. Partner explains why the larger division can be solved without drawing 12 complete grids.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: the official task requires connecting patterns, using a diagram of one whole, translating to a multiplication relationship and reviewing another learner's explanation. Numeric quotient answers alone do not establish a correct grouping model.

KeyConcepts.Title: Count divisor-sized groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: A whole number divided by a positive decimal group size asks how many such groups fit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Smaller divisor yields more groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: A group of size0.02 is ten times smaller than0.2, so there are ten times as many groups for a fixed positive total.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use inverse multiplication
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying the number of groups by group size reconstructs original quantity.
KeyConcepts.Example: An exact quotient must satisfy divisor×quotient=dividend.
